urlMetadata.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks

content.text:
Ethan Perez⋆    Aleksandra Piktus†, Fabio Petroni†, Vladimir Karpukhin†, Naman Goyal†, Heinrich Küttler†    Mike Lewis†    Wen-tau Yih†    Tim Rocktäschel    Sebastian Riedel    Douwe Kiela††Facebook AI Research; ‡University College London; ⋆New York University

###### Abstract

Large pre-trained language models have been shown to store factual knowledge in their parameters, and achieve state-of-the-art results when fine-tuned on downstream NLP tasks. However, their ability to access and precisely manipulate knowledge is still limited, and hence on knowledge-intensive tasks, their performance lags behind task-specific architectures. Additionally, providing provenance for their decisions and updating their world knowledge remain open research problems. Pre-trained models with a differentiable access mechanism to explicit non-parametric memory have so far been only investigated for extractive downstream tasks. We explore a general-purpose fine-tuning recipe for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) — models which combine pre-trained parametric and non-parametric memory for language generation. We introduce RAG models where the parametric memory is a pre-trained seq2seq model and the non-parametric memory is a dense vector index of Wikipedia, accessed with a pre-trained neural retriever. We compare two RAG formulations, one which conditions on the same retrieved passages across the whole generated sequence, and another which can use different passages per token. We fine-tune and evaluate our models on a wide range of knowledge-intensive NLP tasks and set the state of the art on three open domain QA tasks, outperforming parametric seq2seq models and task-specific retrieve-and-extract architectures. For language generation tasks, we find that RAG models generate more specific, diverse and factual language than a state-of-the-art parametric-only seq2seq baseline.

## 1 Introduction

Pre-trained neural language models have been shown to learn a substantial amount of in-depth knowledge from data \[[47](#bib.bib47)\]. They can do so without any access to an external memory, as a parameterized implicit knowledge base \[[51](#bib.bib51), [52](#bib.bib52)\]. While this development is exciting, such models do have downsides: They cannot easily expand or revise their memory, can’t straightforwardly provide insight into their predictions, and may produce “hallucinations” \[[38](#bib.bib38)\]. Hybrid models that combine parametric memory with non-parametric (i.e., retrieval-based) memories \[[20](#bib.bib20), [26](#bib.bib26), [48](#bib.bib48)\] can address some of these issues because knowledge can be directly revised and expanded, and accessed knowledge can be inspected and interpreted. REALM \[[20](#bib.bib20)\] and ORQA \[[31](#bib.bib31)\], two recently introduced models that combine masked language models \[[8](#bib.bib8)\] with a differentiable retriever, have shown promising results, but have only explored open-domain extractive question answering. Here, we bring hybrid parametric and non-parametric memory to the “workhorse of NLP,” i.e. sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models.

We endow pre-trained, parametric-memory generation models with a non-parametric memory through a general-purpose fine-tuning approach which we refer to as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). We build RAG models where the parametric memory is a pre-trained seq2seq transformer, and the non-parametric memory is a dense vector index of Wikipedia, accessed with a pre-trained neural retriever. We combine these components in a probabilistic model trained end-to-end (Fig. [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks")). The retriever (Dense Passage Retriever \[[26](#bib.bib26)\], henceforth DPR) provides latent documents conditioned on the input, and the seq2seq model (BART \[[32](#bib.bib32)\]) then conditions on these latent documents together with the input to generate the output. We marginalize the latent documents with a top-K approximation, either on a per-output basis (assuming the same document is responsible for all tokens) or a per-token basis (where different documents are responsible for different tokens). Like T5 \[[51](#bib.bib51)\] or BART, RAG can be fine-tuned on any seq2seq task, whereby both the generator and retriever are jointly learned.

There has been extensive previous work proposing architectures to enrich systems with non-parametric memory which are trained from scratch for specific tasks, e.g. memory networks \[[64](#bib.bib64), [55](#bib.bib55)\], stack-augmented networks \[[25](#bib.bib25)\] and memory layers \[[30](#bib.bib30)\]. In contrast, we explore a setting where both parametric and non-parametric memory components are pre-trained and pre-loaded with extensive knowledge. Crucially, by using pre-trained access mechanisms, the ability to access knowledge is present without additional training.

Our results highlight the benefits of combining parametric and non-parametric memory with generation for _knowledge-intensive tasks_—tasks that humans could not reasonably be expected to perform without access to an external knowledge source. Our RAG models achieve state-of-the-art results on open Natural Questions \[[29](#bib.bib29)\], WebQuestions \[[3](#bib.bib3)\] and CuratedTrec \[[2](#bib.bib2)\] and strongly outperform recent approaches that use specialised pre-training objectives on TriviaQA \[[24](#bib.bib24)\]. Despite these being extractive tasks, we find that unconstrained generation outperforms previous extractive approaches. For knowledge-intensive generation, we experiment with MS-MARCO \[[1](#bib.bib1)\] and Jeopardy question generation, and we find that our models generate responses that are more factual, specific, and diverse than a BART baseline. For FEVER \[[56](#bib.bib56)\] fact verification, we achieve results within 4.3% of state-of-the-art pipeline models which use strong retrieval supervision. Finally, we demonstrate that the non-parametric memory can be replaced to update the models’ knowledge as the world changes.11 1 Code to run experiments with RAG has been open-sourced as part of the HuggingFace Transformers Library \[[66](#bib.bib66)\] and can be found at [https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/master/examples/rag/](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/master/examples/rag/). An interactive demo of RAG models can be found at [https://huggingface.co/rag/](https://huggingface.co/rag/)

Figure 1: Overview of our approach. We combine a pre-trained retriever (_Query Encoder_ + _Document Index_) with a pre-trained seq2seq model (_Generator_) and fine-tune end-to-end. For query xx, we use Maximum Inner Product Search (MIPS) to find the top-K documents ziz\_{i}. For final prediction yy, we treat zz as a latent variable and marginalize over seq2seq predictions given different documents.

## 2 Methods

We explore RAG models, which use the input sequence xx to retrieve text documents zz and use them as additional context when generating the target sequence yy. As shown in Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks"), our models leverage two components: (i) a retriever pη​(z|x)p\_{\\eta}(z|x) with parameters η\\eta that returns (top-K truncated) distributions over text passages given a query xx and (ii) a generator pθ(yi|x,z,y1:i−1)p\_{\\theta}(y\_{i}|x,z,y\_{1:i-1}) parametrized by θ\\theta that generates a current token based on a context of the previous i−1i-1 tokens y1:i−1y\_{1:i-1}, the original input xx and a retrieved passage zz.

To train the retriever and generator end-to-end, we treat the retrieved document as a latent variable. We propose two models that marginalize over the latent documents in different ways to produce a distribution over generated text. In one approach, _RAG-Sequence_, the model uses the same document to predict each target token. The second approach, _RAG-Token_, can predict each target token based on a different document. In the following, we formally introduce both models and then describe the pηp\_{\\eta} and pθp\_{\\theta} components, as well as the training and decoding procedure.

### 2.1 Models

#### RAG-Sequence Model

The RAG-Sequence model uses the same retrieved document to generate the complete _sequence_. Technically, it treats the retrieved document as a single latent variable that is marginalized to get the seq2seq probability p⁡(y|x)p(y|x) via a top-K approximation. Concretely, the top K documents are retrieved using the retriever, and the generator produces the output sequence probability for each document, which are then marginalized,

pRAG-Sequence(y|x)≈∑z∈top-k(p(⋅|x))pη(z|x)pθ(y|x,z)\=∑z∈top-k(p(⋅|x))pη(z|x)∏iNpθ(yi|x,z,y1:i−1)p\_{\\text{\\tiny{RAG-Sequence}}}(y|x)\\;\\approx\\;\\sum\_{\\mathclap{z\\in\\text{top-}k(p(\\cdot|x))}}p\_{\\eta}(z|x)p\_{\\theta}(y|x,z)\\;=\\;\\sum\_{\\mathclap{z\\in\\text{top-}k(p(\\cdot|x))}}p\_{\\eta}(z|x)\\prod\_{i}^{N}p\_{\\theta}(y\_{i}|x,z,y\_{1:i-1})

#### RAG-Token Model

In the RAG-Token model we can draw a different latent document for each target _token_ and marginalize accordingly. This allows the generator to choose content from several documents when producing an answer. Concretely, the top K documents are retrieved using the retriever, and then the generator produces a distribution for the next output token for each document, before marginalizing, and repeating the process with the following output token, Formally, we define:

pRAG-Token(y|x)≈∏iN∑z∈top-k(p(⋅|x))pη(z|x)pθ(yi|x,z,y1:i−1)p\_{\\text{\\tiny{RAG-Token}}}(y|x)\\;\\approx\\;\\prod\_{i}^{N}\\;\\sum\_{z\\in\\text{top-}k(p(\\cdot|x))}p\_{\\eta}(z|x)p\_{\\theta}(y\_{i}|x,z,y\_{1:i-1})

Finally, we note that RAG can be used for sequence classification tasks by considering the target class as a target sequence of length one, in which case RAG-Sequence and RAG-Token are equivalent.

### 2.2 Retriever: DPR

The retrieval component pη​(z|x)p\_{\\eta}(z|x) is based on DPR \[[26](#bib.bib26)\]. DPR follows a bi-encoder architecture:

pη​(z|x)∝exp⁡(𝐝​(z)⊤​𝐪​(x))𝐝⁡(z)\=BERTd​(z),𝐪⁡(x)\=BERTq​(x)p\_{\\eta}(z|x)\\propto\\exp\\left(\\mathbf{d}(z)^{\\top}\\mathbf{q}(x)\\right)\\;\\;\\;\\;\\;\\;\\;\\;\\;\\mathbf{d}(z)=\\text{BERT}\_{d}(z),\\;\\;\\mathbf{q}(x)=\\text{BERT}\_{q}(x)

where 𝐝⁡(z)\\mathbf{d}(z) is a dense representation of a document produced by a BERTBASE _document encoder_ \[[8](#bib.bib8)\], and 𝐪⁡(x)\\mathbf{q}(x) a query representation produced by a _query encoder_, also based on BERTBASE. Calculating top-k(pη(⋅|x))\\text{top-k}(p\_{\\eta}(\\cdot|x)), the list of kk documents zz with highest prior probability pη​(z|x)p\_{\\eta}(z|x), is a Maximum Inner Product Search (MIPS) problem, which can be approximately solved in sub-linear time \[[23](#bib.bib23)\]. We use a pre-trained bi-encoder from DPR to initialize our retriever and to build the document index. This retriever was trained to retrieve documents which contain answers to TriviaQA \[[24](#bib.bib24)\] questions and Natural Questions \[[29](#bib.bib29)\]. We refer to the document index as the _non-parametric memory_.

### 2.3 Generator: BART

The generator component pθ(yi|x,z,y1:i−1)p\_{\\theta}(y\_{i}|x,z,y\_{1:i-1}) could be modelled using any encoder-decoder. We use BART-large \[[32](#bib.bib32)\], a pre-trained seq2seq transformer \[[58](#bib.bib58)\] with 400M parameters. To combine the input xx with the retrieved content zz when generating from BART, we simply concatenate them. BART was pre-trained using a denoising objective and a variety of different noising functions. It has obtained state-of-the-art results on a diverse set of generation tasks and outperforms comparably-sized T5 models \[[32](#bib.bib32)\]. We refer to the BART generator parameters θ\\theta as the _parametric memory_ henceforth.

### 2.4 Training

We jointly train the retriever and generator components without any direct supervision on what document should be retrieved. Given a fine-tuning training corpus of input/output pairs (xj,yj)(x\_{j},y\_{j}), we minimize the negative marginal log-likelihood of each target, ∑j−logp(yj|xj)\\sum\_{j}-\\log p(y\_{j}|x\_{j}) using stochastic gradient descent with Adam \[[28](#bib.bib28)\]. Updating the document encoder BERTd\\text{BERT}\_{d} during training is costly as it requires the document index to be periodically updated as REALM does during pre-training \[[20](#bib.bib20)\]. We do not find this step necessary for strong performance, and keep the document encoder (and index) fixed, only fine-tuning the query encoder BERTq\\text{BERT}\_{q} and the BART generator.

### 2.5 Decoding

At test time, RAG-Sequence and RAG-Token require different ways to approximate arg​maxy⁡p​(y|x)\\argmax\_{y}p(y|x).

#### RAG-Token

The RAG-Token model can be seen as a standard, autoregressive seq2seq generator with transition probability: pθ′(yi|x,y1:i−1)\=∑z∈top-k(p(⋅|x))pη(zi|x)pθ(yi|x,zi,y1:i−1)p^{\\prime}\_{\\theta}(y\_{i}|x,y\_{1:i-1})=\\sum\_{z\\in\\text{top-}k(p(\\cdot|x))}p\_{\\eta}(z\_{i}|x)p\_{\\theta}(y\_{i}|x,z\_{i},y\_{1:i-1}) To decode, we can plug pθ′(yi|x,y1:i−1)p^{\\prime}\_{\\theta}(y\_{i}|x,y\_{1:i-1}) into a standard beam decoder.

#### RAG-Sequence

For RAG-Sequence, the likelihood p⁡(y|x)p(y|x) does not break into a conventional per- token likelihood, hence we cannot solve it with a single beam search. Instead, we run beam search for each document zz, scoring each hypothesis using pθ(yi|x,z,y1:i−1)p\_{\\theta}(y\_{i}|x,z,y\_{1:i-1}). This yields a set of hypotheses YY, some of which may not have appeared in the beams of all documents. To estimate the probability of an hypothesis yy we run an additional forward pass for each document zz for which yy does not appear in the beam, multiply generator probability with pη​(z|x)p\_{\\eta}(z|x) and then sum the probabilities across beams for the marginals. We refer to this decoding procedure as “Thorough Decoding.” For longer output sequences, |Y||Y| can become large, requiring many forward passes. For more efficient decoding, we can make a further approximation that pθ​(y|x,zi)≈0p\_{\\theta}(y|x,z\_{i})\\approx 0 where yy was not generated during beam search from x,zix,z\_{i}. This avoids the need to run additional forward passes once the candidate set YY has been generated. We refer to this decoding procedure as “Fast Decoding.”

## 3 Experiments

We experiment with RAG in a wide range of knowledge-intensive tasks. For all experiments, we use a single Wikipedia dump for our non-parametric knowledge source. Following [Lee et al. \[31\]](#bib.bib31) and [Karpukhin et al. \[26\]](#bib.bib26), we use the December 2018 dump. Each Wikipedia article is split into disjoint 100-word chunks, to make a total of 21M documents. We use the document encoder to compute an embedding for each document, and build a single MIPS index using FAISS \[[23](#bib.bib23)\] with a Hierarchical Navigable Small World approximation for fast retrieval \[[37](#bib.bib37)\]. During training, we retrieve the top kk documents for each query. We consider k∈{5,10}k\\in\\{5,10\\} for training and set kk for test time using dev data. We now discuss experimental details for each task.

### 3.1 Open-domain Question Answering

Open-domain question answering (QA) is an important real-world application and common testbed for knowledge-intensive tasks \[[20](#bib.bib20)\]. We treat questions and answers as input-output text pairs (x,y)(x,y) and train RAG by directly minimizing the negative log-likelihood of answers. We compare RAG to the popular extractive QA paradigm \[[5](#bib.bib5), [7](#bib.bib7), [31](#bib.bib31), [26](#bib.bib26)\], where answers are extracted spans from retrieved documents, relying primarily on non-parametric knowledge. We also compare to “Closed-Book QA” approaches \[[52](#bib.bib52)\], which, like RAG, generate answers, but which do not exploit retrieval, instead relying purely on parametric knowledge. We consider four popular open-domain QA datasets: Natural Questions (NQ) \[[29](#bib.bib29)\], TriviaQA (TQA) \[[24](#bib.bib24)\]. WebQuestions (WQ) \[[3](#bib.bib3)\] and CuratedTrec (CT) \[[2](#bib.bib2)\]. As CT and WQ are small, we follow DPR \[[26](#bib.bib26)\] by initializing CT and WQ models with our NQ RAG model. We use the same train/dev/test splits as prior work \[[31](#bib.bib31), [26](#bib.bib26)\] and report Exact Match (EM) scores. For TQA, to compare with T5 \[[52](#bib.bib52)\], we also evaluate on the TQA Wiki test set.

### 3.2 Abstractive Question Answering

RAG models can go beyond simple extractive QA and answer questions with free-form, abstractive text generation. To test RAG’s natural language generation (NLG) in a knowledge-intensive setting, we use the MSMARCO NLG task v2.1 \[[43](#bib.bib43)\]. The task consists of questions, ten gold passages retrieved from a search engine for each question, and a full sentence answer annotated from the retrieved passages. We do not use the supplied passages, only the questions and answers, to treat MSMARCO as an open-domain abstractive QA task. MSMARCO has some questions that cannot be answered in a way that matches the reference answer without access to the gold passages, such as “What is the weather in Volcano, CA?” so performance will be lower without using gold passages. We also note that some MSMARCO questions cannot be answered using Wikipedia alone. Here, RAG can rely on parametric knowledge to generate reasonable responses.

### 3.3 Jeopardy Question Generation

To evaluate RAG’s generation abilities in a non-QA setting, we study open-domain question generation. Rather than use questions from standard open-domain QA tasks, which typically consist of short, simple questions, we propose the more demanding task of generating Jeopardy questions. Jeopardy is an unusual format that consists of trying to guess an entity from a fact about that entity. For example, “The World Cup” is the answer to the question “In 1986 Mexico scored as the first country to host this international sports competition twice.” As Jeopardy questions are precise, factual statements, generating Jeopardy questions conditioned on their answer entities constitutes a challenging knowledge-intensive generation task.

We use the splits from SearchQA \[[10](#bib.bib10)\], with 100K train, 14K dev, and 27K test examples. As this is a new task, we train a BART model for comparison. Following \[[67](#bib.bib67)\], we evaluate using the SQuAD-tuned Q-BLEU-1 metric \[[42](#bib.bib42)\]. Q-BLEU is a variant of BLEU with a higher weight for matching entities and has higher correlation with human judgment for question generation than standard metrics. We also perform two human evaluations, one to assess generation factuality, and one for specificity. We define factuality as whether a statement can be corroborated by trusted external sources, and specificity as high mutual dependence between the input and output \[[33](#bib.bib33)\]. We follow best practice and use pairwise comparative evaluation \[[34](#bib.bib34)\]. Evaluators are shown an answer and two generated questions, one from BART and one from RAG. They are then asked to pick one of four options—quuestion A is better, question B is better, both are good, or neither is good.

### 3.4 Fact Verification

FEVER \[[56](#bib.bib56)\] requires classifying whether a natural language claim is supported or refuted by Wikipedia, or whether there is not enough information to decide. The task requires retrieving evidence from Wikipedia relating to the claim and then reasoning over this evidence to classify whether the claim is true, false, or unverifiable from Wikipedia alone. FEVER is a retrieval problem coupled with an challenging entailment reasoning task. It also provides an appropriate testbed for exploring the RAG models’ ability to handle classification rather than generation. We map FEVER class labels (supports, refutes, or not enough info) to single output tokens and directly train with claim-class pairs. Crucially, unlike most other approaches to FEVER, we do not use supervision on retrieved evidence. In many real-world applications, retrieval supervision signals aren’t available, and models that do not require such supervision will be applicable to a wider range of tasks. We explore two variants: the standard 3-way classification task (supports/refutes/not enough info) and the 2-way (supports/refutes) task studied in [Thorne and Vlachos \[57\]](#bib.bib57). In both cases we report label accuracy.

### 4.1 Open-domain Question Answering

Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4 Results ‣ Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks") shows results for RAG along with state-of-the-art models. On all four open-domain QA tasks, RAG sets a new state of the art (only on the T5-comparable split for TQA). RAG combines the generation flexibility of the “closed-book” (parametric only) approaches and the performance of "open-book" retrieval-based approaches. Unlike REALM and T5+SSM, RAG enjoys strong results without expensive, specialized “salient span masking” pre-training \[[20](#bib.bib20)\]. It is worth noting that RAG’s retriever is initialized using DPR’s retriever, which uses retrieval supervision on Natural Questions and TriviaQA. RAG compares favourably to the DPR QA system, which uses a BERT-based “cross-encoder” to re-rank documents, along with an extractive reader. RAG demonstrates that neither a re-ranker nor extractive reader is necessary for state-of-the-art performance.

There are several advantages to generating answers even when it is possible to extract them. Documents with clues about the answer but do not contain the answer verbatim can still contribute towards a correct answer being generated, which is not possible with standard extractive approaches, leading to more effective marginalization over documents. Furthermore, RAG can generate correct answers even when the correct answer is not in any retrieved document, achieving 11.8% accuracy in such cases for NQ, where an extractive model would score 0%.

### 4.2 Abstractive Question Answering

As shown in Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4 Results ‣ Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks"), RAG-Sequence outperforms BART on Open MS-MARCO NLG by 2.6 Bleu points and 2.6 Rouge-L points. RAG approaches state-of-the-art model performance, which is impressive given that (i) those models access gold passages with specific information required to generate the reference answer , (ii) many questions are unanswerable without the gold passages, and (iii) not all questions are answerable from Wikipedia alone. Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.3 Jeopardy Question Generation ‣ 4 Results ‣ Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks") shows some generated answers from our models. Qualitatively, we find that RAG models hallucinate less and generate factually correct text more often than BART. Later, we also show that RAG generations are more diverse than BART generations (see §[4.5](#S4.SS5 "4.5 Additional Results ‣ 4 Results ‣ Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks")).

### 4.3 Jeopardy Question Generation

Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4 Results ‣ Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks") shows that RAG-Token performs better than RAG-Sequence on Jeopardy question generation, with both models outperforming BART on Q-BLEU-1. [5](#S4.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 4.3 Jeopardy Question Generation ‣ 4 Results ‣ Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks") shows human evaluation results, over 452 pairs of generations from BART and RAG-Token. Evaluators indicated that BART was more factual than RAG in only 7.1% of cases, while RAG was more factual in 42.7% of cases, and both RAG and BART were factual in a further 17% of cases, clearly demonstrating the effectiveness of RAG on the task over a state-of-the-art generation model. Evaluators also find RAG generations to be more specific by a large margin. Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.3 Jeopardy Question Generation ‣ 4 Results ‣ Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks") shows typical generations from each model.

Jeopardy questions often contain two separate pieces of information, and RAG-Token may perform best because it can generate responses that combine content from several documents. Figure [2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 4.3 Jeopardy Question Generation ‣ 4 Results ‣ Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks") shows an example. When generating “Sun”, the posterior is high for document 2 which mentions “The Sun Also Rises”. Similarly, document 1 dominates the posterior when “A Farewell to Arms” is generated. Intriguingly, after the first token of each book is generated, the document posterior flattens. This observation suggests that the generator can complete the titles without depending on specific documents. In other words, the model’s parametric knowledge is sufficient to complete the titles. We find evidence for this hypothesis by feeding the BART-only baseline with the partial decoding "The Sun. BART completes the generation "The Sun Also Rises" is a novel by this author of "The Sun Also Rises" indicating the title "The Sun Also Rises" is stored in BART’s parameters. Similarly, BART will complete the partial decoding "The Sun Also Rises" is a novel by this author of "A with "The Sun Also Rises" is a novel by this author of "A Farewell to Arms". This example shows how parametric and non-parametric memories _work together_—the non-parametric component helps to guide the generation, drawing out specific knowledge stored in the parametric memory.

The posterior for document 1 is high when generating “A Farewell to Arms" and for document 2 when generating “The Sun Also Rises".

Table 3: Examples from generation tasks. RAG models generate more specific and factually accurate responses. ‘?’ indicates factually incorrect responses, \* indicates partially correct responses.

Table 4: Human assessments for the Jeopardy Question Generation Task.

### 4.4 Fact Verification

Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4 Results ‣ Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks") shows our results on FEVER. For 3-way classification, RAG scores are within 4.3% of state-of-the-art models, which are complex pipeline systems with domain-specific architectures and substantial engineering, trained using intermediate retrieval supervision, which RAG does not require. For 2-way classification, we compare against [Thorne and Vlachos \[57\]](#bib.bib57), who train RoBERTa \[[35](#bib.bib35)\] to classify the claim as true or false given the gold evidence sentence. RAG achieves an accuracy within 2.7% of this model, despite being supplied with only the claim and retrieving its own evidence. We also analyze whether documents retrieved by RAG correspond to documents annotated as gold evidence in FEVER. We calculate the overlap in article titles between the top kk documents retrieved by RAG and gold evidence annotations. We find that the top retrieved document is from a gold article in 71% of cases, and a gold article is present in the top 10 retrieved articles in 90% of cases.

### 4.5 Additional Results

#### Generation Diversity

Section [4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Jeopardy Question Generation ‣ 4 Results ‣ Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks") shows that RAG models are more factual and specific than BART for Jeopardy question generation. Following recent work on diversity-promoting decoding \[[33](#bib.bib33), [59](#bib.bib59), [39](#bib.bib39)\], we also investigate generation diversity by calculating the ratio of distinct ngrams to total ngrams generated by different models. Table [5](#S4.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 4.3 Jeopardy Question Generation ‣ 4 Results ‣ Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks") shows that RAG-Sequence’s generations are more diverse than RAG-Token’s, and both are significantly more diverse than BART without needing any diversity-promoting decoding.

Table 6: Ablations on the dev set. As FEVER is a classification task, both RAG models are equivalent.

#### Retrieval Ablations

A key feature of RAG is learning to retrieve relevant information for the task. To assess the effectiveness of the retrieval mechanism, we run ablations where we freeze the retriever during training. As shown in Table [6](#S4.T6 "Table 6 ‣ Generation Diversity ‣ 4.5 Additional Results ‣ 4 Results ‣ Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks"), learned retrieval improves results for all tasks.

from math import comb, sqrt

def fisher_two_sided(a,b,c,d):
    # [[a,b],[c,d]]
    n=a+b+c+d
    def p(a,b,c,d):
        return comb(a+b,a)*comb(c+d,c)/comb(n,a+c)
    obs=p(a,b,c,d)
    total=0.0
    for i in range(0, min(a+b,a+c)+1):
        j=a+b-i; k=a+c-i; l=c+d-k
        if j<0 or k<0 or l<0: continue
        pi=p(i,j,k,l)
        if pi <= obs + 1e-12: total += pi
    return total

def wilson(k,n,z=1.96):
    if n==0: return (None,None)
    ph=k/n; den=1+z*z/n
    centre=(ph+z*z/(2*n))/den
    half=z*sqrt(ph*(1-ph)/n + z*z/(4*n*n))/den
    return (centre-half, centre+half)

# Feynman 0.5.65 as an evaluation instrument **A dogfooded case study of an AI research harness, judged by AI-eval-quality criteria** - **Date:** 2026-11-14 - **Harness under study:** Feynman `0.5.65` (installed), repository HEAD `0.5.69` - **Study type:** static audit + deterministic meta-eval + one runtime verification probe - **Canonical artifact:** `outputs/feynman-harness-eval-quality-case-study.md` - **Raw artifacts:** `experiments/eval-scorer-probe.mjs`, `experiments/eval-scorer-probe-results.json`, `experiments/score-verifier-output.mjs`, `experiments/verifier-output-score.json`, `outputs/.probes/` --- ## 0. Scope and method This is a case study of Feynman as an **evaluation instrument**, not a benchmark of its research prose. The question is: when Feynman reports that a research workflow scored 100%, what has actually been measured, how repeatable is it, and what would a careful eval engineer conclude? I used four kinds of evidence: 1. **Static audit** of the installed package, the public repository, the workflow prompts, the four bundled subagents, and the `evals/` directory. 2. **Deterministic meta-eval** of Feynman's own citation scorer: eight synthetic outputs with known ground truth, plus probes of the `done` metric and the aggregate table. The scorer was imported from a generated copy of `evals/run.mjs` with only the CLI entrypoint removed; no scoring logic was reimplemented. 3. **Runtime verification probe**: a short draft with one fabricated paper, one false quantitative claim, one false directional claim, one dead URL, one uncited true claim, and two true citations, given to Feynman's `verifier` subagent in a clean workspace. The first attempt was contaminated by probe fixtures in the same workspace and is reported as a negative control, not as a capability measurement. 4. **Re-analysis of the seven committed result files** in `evals/results/`, including their recorded git SHA, dirty flag, version, token usage, and per-row failures. **Explicit non-goals:** I did not run the full 12-question eval (it would cost millions of tokens per question and hours of wall time), did not recruit human raters, and did not inspect Feynman's private telemetry or internal eval history. The study is therefore a close reading of the public instrument plus small controlled probes, not a leaderboard run. A reflexivity warning applies throughout: I am the harness being studied. I read `evals/questions.jsonl` before designing the probes. The deterministic probes are resistant to that observer effect because their expectations are fixed in code; the runtime verifier probe is not blinded and is reported as `n=1`. --- ## 1. Executive summary **What is good.** Feynman ships a real research-quality eval, not a vibes-based demo. It uses deterministic checks against arXiv, Crossref, and doi.org, with no LLM judge. Each question runs in an isolated temp workspace and isolated `FEYNMAN_HOME`, with telemetry off. Every row records the git SHA, dirty flag, Feynman version, model, wall time, token usage, failures, and the workdir containing the full session. Failures are kept in the results rather than deleted. The README states its own limitations ("Treat a single run as noisy"; "read the listed rows before calling something a hallucination"). These are practices many agent evals do not have. **What is measured.** The headline metrics are bibliographic: whether cited arXiv IDs and DOIs resolve, whether the resolved title appears near the identifier, whether expected key papers are present, and whether the final output plus a provenance sidecar exist. They do **not** measure whether the sentence attached to a citation is true. A sentence that says a paper found the *opposite* of its central claim still scores 100% on title match, because the title tokens are present and the negation is invisible to a bag-of-words overlap check. **What the committed evidence shows.** In all 22 committed rows, citation validity is 100% in every row that has citations, and key-paper recall is 100% in every completed row. The only variation is completion: 4/4, 3/4, 2/4, 2/2, and one 45-minute timeout. The eval has never registered an unresolved citation in a completed run. Title match is 97–100%, with five mismatches across two rows. In other words, on the public record the eval is primarily a **completion detector** with a bibliographic sanity check, not a research-quality gradient. **Provenance is weaker than the table suggests.** The headline 0.5.3 runs were made on a **dirty tree** (`git_dirty: true`) at commit `c1e0b29`, whose `package.json` says `0.5.2`; the recorded version field says `0.5.3`. The commit that adds the `bg_wait` rule the summary says was included is a *descendant* of that eval commit. One committed result row references a git SHA (`d926547`) that does not exist in the public repository. The workdirs are local macOS paths under `/Users/advaitpaliwal/...` or `/var/folders/...`, so `--rescore` cannot be reproduced from the repository alone. **Cadence and statistics are thin.** The last committed eval result is dated 2026-09-24 and scored 0.5.3-era prompts. Since then, 66 release sections (0.5.4–0.5.69) and 10 commits touching `prompts/`, `.feynman/agents/`, `.feynman/SYSTEM.md`, or `skills/` have landed. There is no reference to `evals/` in `.github/workflows/` or in any `package.json` script, so the eval is manual. Each configuration was run once on four questions. A 4/4 versus 3/4 completion difference is not statistically distinguishable (Fisher exact two-sided *p* = 1.0; Wilson 95% CI for 4/4 is [0.51, 1.00]). **Cost is unmeasured.** Every committed table reports `$0.00` because the provider entry in `models.json` has no `cost` block. Token counts are large and heavy-tailed: 3.34M tokens per question for the 0.5.3 Terra run, 5.48M for the 0.5.3 Opus run, and 18.05M for the baseline's timed-out q10. A failed question consumed 28% of its run's tokens. **The runtime verifier is better than the eval that measures it.** In a clean workspace, the `verifier` subagent caught the fabricated arXiv ID, corrected the false RAG claim with the paper's actual 44.5 vs. 34.5 exact-match numbers, removed the fabricated 94.2%, flagged the dead URL, and added a missing DOI/PubMed source. It did this in 82 seconds for 594,620 tokens and $0.0174 (session-reported). But its corrections are largely invisible to the eval scorer. Worse, a transparent verifier that documents a removed fake ID in a "Removed Unsupported Claims" section is *penalized* by the scorer, while a verifier that silently deletes the fake scores higher: 75% vs. 100% citation validity in the controlled probe. **Bottom line.** Feynman's eval is a credible **citation-integrity smoke test** with unusually good isolation and trace capture. It is not yet a research-quality eval: it lacks claim-level faithfulness, human calibration, repeated runs, a private holdout, cost accounting, and a release gate. Its own roadmap says as much: the README lists ScholarQA-CS2, DeepResearch Bench FACT, and SciCoQA as "next lanes, not built yet." --- ## 2. The object: what the eval actually is The eval lives in `evals/`, is added by commit `9b41eec` (2026-09-23), and is explicitly **not** included in the npm package (`package.json` `files` omits `evals/`; `evals/README.md` says so). + provenance sidecar] A --> S[deterministic scorer] S --> M[citation validity
title overlap
key-paper recall] M --> R[result JSONL + Markdown table] ``` A crucial design choice: the eval measures the **artifact**, not the transcript. It reads the final Markdown, extracts arXiv IDs and DOIs, resolves them, and compares titles. It does not score the reasoning, the search path, the quality of the sources, or the truth of the prose. ### 2.1 The 12-question set | ID | Field | Question | Source | |---|---|---|---| | q01 | ML | test-time compute scaling for LLM reasoning | Feynman search benchmark | | q02 | ML | speculative decoding for LLM inference | Feynman search benchmark | | q03 | interpretability | sparse autoencoders for mechanistic interpretability | Feynman search benchmark | | q04 | genome editing | CRISPR base editing | Feynman search benchmark | | q05 | ML | mixture-of-experts routing | Feynman search benchmark | | q06 | NLP | retrieval-augmented generation | Feynman search benchmark | | q07 | genomics | enhancer–promoter compatibility, human vs. Drosophila | LitQA2 | | q08 | single-cell methods | tagmentation of cDNA directly in PCR mix | LitQA2 | | q09 | computational chemistry | Wyckoff-site constraints in symmetric MD | LitQA2 | | q10 | econometrics | difference-in-differences with staggered timing | hand-authored | | q11 | earth science | ML medium-range global weather forecasting | hand-authored | | q12 | cosmology | the Hubble tension | hand-authored | **Observation:** every committed result file uses only q01, q04, q07, and q10. The 0.5.3 Opus run uses q01 and q10. **Eight of the 12 questions (q02, q03, q05, q06, q08, q09, q11, q12) have no committed result.** The "12-question eval" is a design; the executed public benchmark is a four-question subset. --- ## 3. Strengths: what an eval engineer should copy These are not consolations. They are the parts of the harness that are genuinely better than the median agent eval. 1. **No LLM judge for the headline metric.** Citation validity and title match are deterministic. This avoids position, verbosity, and self-enhancement biases documented for LLM judges [6]. It also makes the scorer cheap to rerun. 2. **Per-question isolation.** Each run gets a fresh temp workspace and its own `FEYNMAN_HOME`, so one question cannot contaminate another through files or config. This is the right default and is exactly what my first verifier probe violated. 3. **Trace capture.** The result row records `git_sha`, `git_dirty`, `feynman_version`, model, `workdir`, per-question token usage, and the full session JSONL. That is enough to audit a run after the fact, even if the workdir is later deleted. 4. **Failures are retained.** Timed-out and incomplete rows are written to the JSONL and shown in the Markdown table rather than dropped. The baseline's 45-minute q10 timeout is visible, not hidden. 5. **Frozen-set discipline.** The README says: keep the set fixed; if you must change a question, bump the id rather than reuse one. That is the correct rule for longitudinal comparison. 6. **Self-aware caveats.** The README says a single run is noisy, tells the reader to inspect listed failures before calling something a hallucination, and lists the next metric lanes that are not built. This is unusually honest documentation. 7. **Low-cost verifier.** A verification pass on a six-paragraph draft cost 594,620 tokens and $0.0174 on `deepseek-v4.1-flash` in this environment. That is cheap enough to run on every draft, which is the right operating point for a verification layer. --- ## 4. Construct validity: what the numbers mean This is the central issue. The eval's metrics are sensible for what they measure, but the construct "research quality" is much larger than the measured construct "bibliographic integrity." | Metric | Code behavior | Measures | Does **not** measure | |---|---|---|---| | `done` | A final `outputs/.md` exists and a same-stem `.provenance.md` exists | Artifact production | Whether either file has content, or whether provenance fields are true | | `cites` | Distinct arXiv IDs and DOIs extracted by regex | Identifier-bearing citation density | Web citations, author–year citations, citation quality | | `valid` | Fraction of checked IDs that resolve via arXiv/Crossref/doi.org | Identifier existence | Whether the source supports the attached claim | | `title` | Resolved title tokens overlap the line carrying the ID by ≥60%, or first-author surname appears | Bibliographic consistency | Claim truth, negation, scope, numbers, causality | | `recall` | Expected key papers appear by ID or exact normalized title | Coverage of a fixed key set | Comprehensiveness beyond the key set, synthesis quality | | `wall`, `tokens`, `cost` | Summed over parent and subagent sessions | Resource use | Cost-effectiveness, because `cost` is often 0 | | — | — | — | Claim-level faithfulness, factual accuracy of uncited prose, source quality, novelty, reasoning, human preference | ### 4.1 The scorer's blind spots, demonstrated I ran eight synthetic outputs through the actual `scoreCitations` function. All eight behaved as the code predicts; three of those behaviors are gaps. | Probe | Input | Expected scorer behavior | Observed | Verdict | |---|---|---|---|---| | P1 | Real arXiv ID + correct title | resolves, title match | `valid=1`, `title=1` | correct | | P2 | Real ID + wrong paper title | resolves, title mismatch | `valid=1`, `title=0` | correct | | P3 | Fabricated arXiv ID | unresolved | `valid=0`, listed in `unresolved` | correct | | P4 | Real ID + correct title + sentence that **negates** the paper's central claim | scorer passes it | `valid=1`, `title=1` | **gap** | | P5 | Author–year citation with no DOI/arXiv ID | no citation counted | `cites=0`, `valid=null` | **gap** | | P6 | Resolving DOI + unrelated title | resolves, title mismatch | `valid=1`, `title=0` | correct | | P7 | Same ID cited twice | deduplicated | `cites=1` | correct | | P8 | Web source cited by URL only | no citation counted | `cites=0` | **gap** | P4 is the important one. The input was: > Snell et al. (2024), *Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters*, arXiv:2408.03314, find that test-time compute is **never** more effective than scaling model parameters. The scorer sees the full title, 100% token overlap, and returns `title=1`. The sentence says the opposite of the title. A bag-of-words title check cannot represent negation, attribution, scope, or numeric support. P5 and P8 matter for the workflows the eval claims to cover. `/deepresearch` is supposed to synthesize web sources as well as papers, but a report whose citations are all author–year or URL-based produces `cites=0` and `valid=null`. The table then displays `-` for validity, not `0%`. ### 4.2 Zero-citation rows are not penalized The aggregate table computes `mean` over numeric values only: ```js const mean = (xs) => { const v = xs.filter((x) => typeof x === "number"); ... } ``` A row with `citations=0`, `citation_validity=null`, and `key_recall=1` therefore contributes nothing to the validity or title averages. In a two-row probe (`zero-cites` and `one-cite`), the aggregate printed: | id | done | cites | valid | title | recall | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | zero-cites | yes | 0 | - | - | 100% | | one-cite | yes | 1 | 100% | 100% | 100% | | **all** | 100% | 1 | **100%** | **100%** | 100% | The "all" row reports 100% citation validity even though one of the two reports had **zero checkable citations**. This is not a hypothetical: P5/P8 show how a report can reach that state, and the committed results already contain rows with `citations=0` (the failed runs). Those rows are saved from lowering the citation averages because their validity is `null`. ### 4.3 `done` is file existence, not provenance quality `findFinal` selects a final output only if a same-stem provenance file exists: ```js .existsSync(join(dir, f.replace(/\.md$/, ".provenance.md"))) ``` It does not read the provenance file. In a controlled probe: | Case | `done` | Picked | |---|---|---| | Non-empty final + **empty** provenance | `true` | `outputs/x.md` | | Non-empty final, no provenance | `false` | — | | **Empty** final + empty provenance | `true` | `outputs/x.md` | A zero-byte report with a zero-byte sidecar passes the completion criterion. The `/lit` and `/deepresearch` prompts tell the lead agent to write a provenance record with counts and verification status, but nothing in the scorer checks that those fields exist, are non-empty, or are true. ### 4.4 The transparency penalty This is the most consequential scorer behavior I found. I scored the unverified probe draft, the clean verifier's corrected output, and a counterfactual in which the fake ID is silently deleted without being named in a removal note: | Version | What changed | `cites` | `valid` | `title` | |---|---|---|---|---| | Draft | Contains fake ID, false claim, false number, dead URL | 3 | **66.7%** | 100% | | Clean verified | Fake removed **and named** in "Removed Unsupported Claims"; false number corrected; dead URL removed; real DOI added | 4 | **75.0%** | 100% | | Clean verified, silent deletion | Same corrections, but the fake ID string is not mentioned | 3 | **100%** | 100% | The corrected report improves from 66.7% to 75.0%, but only because the verifier **added** a real DOI. The fake ID is still extracted from the removal note and remains in the denominator. If the verifier had deleted the fake paragraph without documenting it, the report would score 100%. A verifier that follows the `verifier.md` instruction to add a "Removed Unsupported Claims" section is therefore punished relative to one that hides its work. This is a metric-design bug with a clear fix: exclude IDs that appear only in a removal/appendix section, or tag them as `removed` and report them separately. The current behavior creates an incentive against transparent correction. --- ## 5. The metric has zero observed variance in the public record. That may mean the outputs are genuinely well-cited; it also means the metric has not demonstrated the ability to detect a bad citation outside the synthetic probe. **Key-paper recall is a completion indicator, not a quality gradient.** In every completed row, `key_recall = 1.0`; in every incomplete row, `key_recall = 0.0`. It does not distinguish a strong report from a weak one on this set. **Title match is the only metric with observed variance:** five mismatches across two rows (two in the baseline q01, three in the 0.5.3 Opus q10). The README itself warns that short-name citations miss this check, so even these five are not necessarily errors. **The before/after comparison is underpowered.** The final 0.5.3 Terra run completed 4/4; the pre-wait 0.5.2 run completed 3/4. Fisher exact two-sided *p* = 1.0. The final 0.5.3 Opus run completed 2/2; the pre-wait 0.5.2 Opus run completed 2/4; *p* = 0.43. With four questions and one run per arm, the eval cannot distinguish the prompt change from noise. The Wilson 95% CI for 4/4 is [0.51, 1.00]. **Cost is not measured.** Every table says `$0.00` because the `models.json` entry has no `cost` block. The README documents this: "Cost is 0 when the provider's models.json entry has no cost block." Tokens are the only resource signal, and they are heavy-tailed: | Configuration | Tokens / question | Wall / question | |---|---|---| | 0.5.3 Terra | 3,338,449 | 627s | | 0.5.3 Opus | 5,476,520 | 1,100s | | 0.5.0 Sonnet 5 baseline | 18,047,545 | 1,974s | | 0.5.2 pre-wait Terra | 3,518,454 | 681s | | 0.5.2 pre-wait Opus | 3,259,990 | 615s | The baseline's q10 timeout consumed 18,029,830 tokens (25.0% of that run's 72.2M) and produced no output. The pre-wait Terra q04 failure consumed 3,968,890 tokens (28.2% of 14.1M) and produced no output. A single failed question can dominate the cost of a run; a cost-blind table hides that. **The version labels do not agree.** The file `2026-09-24-lit-0.5.3-pre-wait-...` records `feynman_version: 0.5.2`. The summary at the top of `2026-09-24-lit-0.5.3-ferrylane-openai_gpt-5.6-terra.md` says "Compare with the 0.5.2 run in 2026-09-24-lit-ferrylane-openai_gpt-5.6-terra.md", but that file's rows record `feynman_version: 0.5.0` and a SHA that is absent from the repository. These are reporting defects, not research defects, but they matter for an instrument whose job is provenance. ### 5.3 The provenance problem in one paragraph The 0.5.3 headline runs were made at `c1e0b29` with `git_dirty: true`. That commit's `package.json` says `0.5.2`; the result rows say `0.5.3`. The commit that adds the `bg_wait` rule the summary says was included (`b1c4231`) is a **descendant** of `c1e0b29`, so the artifact cannot establish whether the tested tree contained that rule or whether it was an uncommitted local edit. The eval did the right thing by recording `git_dirty`; the process did not do the right thing by running the headline comparison on a dirty tree. A reader who wants to reproduce "0.5.3 = 100%" cannot reconstruct the exact code from the recorded SHA. --- ## 6. Meta-eval: probing the scorer All probe code and raw output: - `experiments/eval-scorer-probe.mjs` - `experiments/eval-scorer-probe-results.json` - `experiments/eval-scorer-probe.log` - `experiments/score-verifier-output.mjs` - `experiments/verifier-output-score.json` - `experiments/eval-stats.log` The scorer source was `evals/run.mjs` at repository HEAD `1174429`, blob SHA-256 `23ba3bff8aa87dc189ef899ee7be680eba63e2818acf8f1dc5e452c410d72a42` (file last changed 2026-09-24, commit `8e7efc5`). The probes import a generated copy with `main()` removed and the helpers exported. No formula, threshold, or regex was rewritten. ### 6.1 Coverage of the probe suite | Claim under test | Probe | Result | |---|---|---| | Valid ID + matching title passes | P1 | pass | | Wrong title is caught | P2, P6 | pass | | Fabricated ID is caught | P3 | pass | | Negation is invisible | P4 | gap | | Author–year citations are invisible | P5 | gap | | URL-only citations are invisible | P8 | gap | | Duplicate IDs are deduplicated | P7 | pass | | Zero-citation rows are not penalized | table probe | gap | | Empty provenance passes `done` | done probe | gap | | Empty final passes `done` | done probe | gap | | Transparent removal is penalized | verifier-output score | gap | 8/8 probes matched their expected scorer behavior; the expectations themselves encode the gaps. This is a useful distinction: the scorer is **implemented as designed**, but the design is too narrow for the construct. ### 6.2 What the probe does and does not establish It establishes that the scorer's behavior follows directly from its code: title-token overlap, ID resolution, null-skipping averages, and file-existence checks. It does not establish the base rate of claim-level errors in real Feynman outputs. That would require a labeled sample of claims and a human or calibrated judge. The probe is a existence proof of blind spots, not an estimate of their frequency. --- ## 7. Runtime verification: a clean dogfood probe The `verifier` agent prompt is the strongest epistemic artifact in the harness. It requires inline citations, URL resolution, two-index DOI/arXiv cross-checks, meaning verification ("A citation is valid only if the source actually supports the specific number, quote, or conclusion attached to it"), removal of unsourced claims, and no fake certainty. The question is whether the runtime behavior matches the prompt, and whether the eval can see the difference. ### 7.1 Fixture and ground truth The fixture (`outputs/.probes/verifier-probe-draft.md`) contains six paragraphs: | # | Claim | Ground truth | |---|---|---| | 1 | Lewis et al. 2020, RAG, arXiv:2005.11401, dense retriever + seq2seq, SOTA on three QA tasks | true | | 2 | The same paper says RAG **underperforms** closed-book on all three tasks and scores **94.2%** EM on NQ | false; abstract says SOTA, and Table 1 reports 44.5 (RAG-Seq) / 44.1 (RAG-Token) vs. 34.5 (T5-11B) | | 3 | [related work], *Retrieval Calibration for Long-Context Scientific Synthesis*, arXiv:2409.99999, +31% citation precision | fabricated ID and paper | | 4 | Vaswani et al. 2017, *Attention Is All You Need*, arXiv:1706.03762, Transformer without recurrence/convolution | true | | 5 | Komor et al. 2016, base editing without double-strand breaks | true, but no identifier | | 6 | Feynman eval documented at `feynman.is/docs/evals/research-quality`, 12 questions, validity 71%→100% from 0.5.0 to 0.5.3 | URL is 404; 12 questions is true from the repo but not verifiable from the web; 71%→100% is false (committed validity was 100% in both) | ### 7.2 Clean run result The clean run used a fresh `/tmp` workspace containing only `draft.md`; the transcript contains zero references to the probe fixtures or the study workspace. It ran on `openrouter/deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017`, the same model as the lead in this session. Session-reported usage: 594,620 tokens, $0.0174, 31 tool calls, 82 seconds. Manual rubric (n=1, not blinded): | Criterion | Result | Evidence | |---|---|---| | Fabricated paper removed or flagged | PASS | Removed; "arXiv has no record of 2409.99999, and a Semantic Scholar title search returned zero results" | | False directional claim corrected | PASS | Replaced with 44.5/44.1 vs. 34.5 and "outperforming parametric seq2seq models" | | False 94.2% removed | PASS | "the value 94.2 does not appear in the paper" | | Dead URL flagged | PASS | Removed paragraph; "returns HTTP 404; no archived copy or indexed eval page was found" | | True claims retained | PASS | Lewis, Vaswani, Komor all retained | | Uncited true claim given a source | PASS | Komor DOI + PMID added | | Unsupported 71%→100% removed | PASS | Removed with the paragraph | | Inline citations + Sources, no orphans | PASS | 3 sources, [1]–[3] all cited | | No new fabricated sources | PASS | arXiv + DOI + PubMed records resolve | | Input draft unmodified | PASS | SHA-256 identical before/after | The verifier also demonstrated a precision/recall tradeoff: it removed the true "12 questions" fact because it could not verify it from the web, even though the repository contains `evals/questions.jsonl` with 12 entries. Under its instructions ("if a factual claim cannot be traced to any source in the research files, either find a source for it or remove it"), removal was correct. But a research report that deletes true-but-unverifiable context is less comprehensive, and the eval's `key_recall` would not notice because "12 questions" is not a key paper. ### 7.3 The contaminated run is the more instructive one The first verifier run used `/work` as its workspace, where my probe fixtures (`experiments/eval-scorer-probe.mjs`, `eval-scorer-probe-results.json`) were present. The verifier found them, used P3 to identify the fake paper, and wrote in its output: "The same title/ID pair appears in the local probe fixture as a deliberately fabricated citation (`experiments/eval-scorer-probe.mjs`, probe P3)." Nine transcript references to `eval-scorer-probe` confirm the leak. That run is **not** a capability measurement; it is a demonstration of fixture leakage. It also shows why the harness's own per-question isolation matters: an eval that leaves its answer key or probe fixtures in the agent's workspace measures the agent's ability to find the answer key. The clean rerun is the one reported above. A second contamination channel is model-level: the 12 questions and their expected key papers are public in the repository, and most key papers are famous. A model that memorized "Snell 2024 = 2408.03314" can satisfy `key_recall` without retrieval. The eval has no private holdout, no canary, and no post-cutoff question set. This is the classic benchmark-overfitting risk identified by Kapoor et al. [1]. --- ## 8. Reliability, contamination, and reporting ### 8.1 Reliability | Property | Status | Evidence | |---|---|---| | Repeated runs per configuration | none | one row per question per config | | Confidence intervals | none in results | I computed Wilson CI for 4/4: [0.51, 1.00] | | Paired comparisons | partial | same four questions, but different subsets for Opus | | Statistical test | none | 4/4 vs. 3/4 Fisher *p* = 1.0; 4/4 vs. 2/4 *p* = 0.43 | | Model variance | none | one model per run; all agents inherit it | | Prompt/runtime ablation | confounded | prompt changes ship with Pi/runtime updates in the same releases | | Timeout sensitivity | high | one 45-minute timeout; 18M tokens | | Cost variance | unmeasured | `$0.00` in every table | The eval is a **single-shot smoke test**. That is a legitimate design for a pre-release check, but it is not enough to support "0.5.3 is better than 0.5.2" or "100% citation validity" as stable properties. ### 8.2 Contamination | Channel | Risk | Current control | |---|---|---| | Public questions + expected papers | high for famous papers | none; questions are committed | | Public LitQA2 items | medium | none; three items are redistributed | | Repo access during a run | low in the eval's isolated workspace, high in a normal repo checkout | eval uses a temp workspace; normal runs do not | | Probe/fixture leakage | demonstrated | none in the harness; my first probe failed this | | Model memorization | high for classics | none; no private holdout | | Canary/held-out set | absent | none | The eval's isolation protects against **cross-question** contamination, not **training-data** contamination. The README's "keep the set fixed" rule preserves comparability but also preserves saturation. ### 8.3 Reporting | Issue | Observation | |---|---| | Headline hides denominators | table shows `valid` but not `citations_checked`; in committed rows they are equal, so no observed inflation, but the code excludes failed lookups | | Headline hides failure detail | `unresolved` and `title_mismatch` are in JSONL but not in the Markdown table | | Cost is zero | no `cost` block in `models.json`; token counts are the only resource signal | | Version labels disagree | filenames/README say 0.5.3/0.5.2; JSONL says 0.5.3/0.5.2/0.5.0; one SHA is absent | | Dirty trees | 4 of 6 result files record `git_dirty: true` | | Workdirs are local | macOS `/Users/...` and `/var/folders/...` paths; `--rescore` is not portable | | Eval not shipped | `package.json` `files` omits `evals/`; users cannot run the vendor's eval from the installed package | | No CI gate | no `evals/` reference in `.github/workflows/` or `package.json` scripts | ### 8.4 Cadence The last committed eval result is 2026-09-24. The repository now contains 66 release sections after 0.5.3 (0.5.4 through 0.5.69) and 10 commits touching the prompts, agents, system prompt, or skills after the last eval commit. There is no automated gate. The README's own rule — "Run the eval before and after any change to prompts ... tools, extensions, or the Pi version" — is a manual convention, and the commit history shows it has not been followed for the last two months of releases. This is the single highest-leverage process fix. An eval that is not run on the change it is meant to guard is documentation, not measurement. --- ## 9. Scorecard Author judgment, grounded in the evidence above. "Strong" means the property is designed and demonstrated; "adequate" means present but thin; "weak" means present but not discriminating; "absent" means not implemented. | Criterion | Rating | Why | |---|---|---| | Construct validity | **weak** | Measures bibliographic integrity, not claim faithfulness or research quality | | Criterion validity (vs. experts) | **absent** | No human ratings, no agreement study, no correlation with expert judgment | | Reliability / variance | **weak** | One run per config, four questions, no CIs | | Reproducibility | **mixed** | Deterministic scorer, SHA/version/dirty captured, isolated runs; but dirty trees, a dangling SHA, local-only workdirs, not shipped, no CI | | Contamination resistance | **weak** | Public fixed set, famous key papers, no private holdout or canary | | Cost accounting | **absent** | `$0.00` everywhere; tokens only | | Reporting / uncertainty | **mixed** | Raw JSONL and failures retained; table hides denominators, cost, and version mismatches | | Coverage | **weak** | 4 of 12 questions exercised; 8 never run in the committed record | | Runtime verification | **promising, unmeasured** | Verifier prompt is strong; clean probe passed 10/10; same-model judge, n=1; eval does not measure it | | Process integration | **weak** | No CI gate; eval stale since 2026-09-24 while 66 releases landed | **Overall:** a good **citation-integrity smoke test** with strong isolation and trace capture, wearing the label of a research-quality eval. The gap is not incompetence; the README names the missing lanes. The gap is between what the instrument measures and what its headline numbers are used to imply. --- ## 10. Recommendations Prioritized by eval-quality leverage, not implementation cost. ### P0 — make the headline honest 1. **Add a claim-level faithfulness metric.** For a sample of cited sentences, check whether the source supports the specific number, quote, or conclusion. Use an NLI model or an LLM judge, but calibrate it against at least 100 human-labeled claims and report agreement. Report claim precision separately from identifier validity. This is the difference between "the citation exists" and "the citation supports the sentence." ReportBench [4] and DeepResearch Bench [3] provide usable framings. 2. **Report denominators in the headline table:** `citations_checked / citations`, `unresolved`, `title_mismatch`, and the number of claims sampled for faithfulness. Never average `null` as if it were a score. 3. **Require a cost block.** If `cost` is missing, mark the run `UNPRICED` rather than `$0.00`. Report cost per completed question and cost per accepted claim. 4. **Exclude removed IDs from citation counts.** Parse "Removed Unsupported Claims" sections and tag those IDs as `removed`, not `unresolved`. Otherwise transparency is penalized (demonstrated: 75% vs. 100%). 5. **Add a private holdout and a rotating public set.** At least 20 held-out questions, post-cutoff where possible, with key papers not in the training distribution. Keep a public subset for comparability; score both and report the gap. 6. **Run each configuration at least three times** on a fixed subset and report median + interval. A single 4/4 is compatible with a true completion rate anywhere from 51% to 100%. ### P1 — make the instrument reproducible and binding 7. **CI gate on prompt/agent/tool changes.** Run a 4-question smoke subset on every PR that touches `prompts/`, `.feynman/agents/`, `.feynman/SYSTEM.md`, `skills/`, `evals/`, or the Pi runtime; run the full set before a release. Store the result artifact and fail closed if it is missing. 8. **Run on clean, tagged trees.** Refuse to publish a headline result with `git_dirty: true`; if a dirty run is exploratory, label it `EXPLORATORY` and do not compare it to a tagged run. 9. **Ship the eval or a container that runs it.** The npm package omits `evals/`; a user cannot reproduce the vendor's claim from the installed artifact. A pinned container with the model gateway config and question set would fix this. 10. **Make workdirs portable.** Commit the final outputs, provenance sidecars, session JSONLs, and scorer inputs (or a content-addressed archive) so `--rescore` works on another machine. 11. **Validate provenance sidecars.** Require non-empty `date`, `sources consulted`, `sources accepted`, `sources rejected`, `verification`, `plan`, and `research files`; fail `done` if the sidecar is empty or missing fields. The current check is file existence only. 12. **Reject empty outputs.** A zero-byte final should not count as `done`. ### P2 — broaden the construct 13. **Extract web and author–year citations.** The current regex sees only arXiv IDs and DOIs; a web-heavy `/deepresearch` report can score `cites=0`. 14. **Add a comprehensiveness metric** beyond key-paper recall: section coverage against the question's expected facets, or an expert rubric. 15. **Add a judge-calibration set.** If an LLM judge is used for faithfulness, measure its agreement with humans and report position/verbosity controls [6]. 16. **Add a contamination canary.** Include at least one question whose answer cannot be memorized (post-cutoff or private), and report performance separately. 17. **Separate prompt and runtime ablations.** Pin the Pi version and model; change one variable at a time. The current release notes bundle prompt changes with Pi updates, so attribution is impossible. --- ## 11. Worse, a transparent verifier that documents a removed fake ID in a "Removed Unsupported Claims" section is *penalized* by the scorer, while a verifier that silently deletes the fake scores higher: 75% vs. 100% citation validity in the controlled probe. **Bottom line.** Feynman's eval is a credible **citation-integrity smoke test** with unusually good isolation and trace capture. It is not yet a research-quality eval: it lacks claim-level faithfulness, human calibration, repeated runs, a private holdout, cost accounting, and a release gate. Its own roadmap says as much: the README lists ScholarQA-CS2, DeepResearch Bench FACT, and SciCoQA as "next lanes, not built yet." --- ## 2. The object: what the eval actually is The eval lives in `evals/`, is added by commit `9b41eec` (2026-09-23), and is explicitly **not** included in the npm package (`package.json` `files` omits `evals/`; `evals/README.md` says so). It is a repository-only instrument. | Component | What it does | Evidence | |---|---|---| | `evals/questions.jsonl` | 12 fixed questions with expected key papers and a `source` field | 6 from Feynman's paper-discovery benchmark, 3 verbatim LitQA2 items, 3 hand-authored | | `evals/run.mjs` | Runs `/lit` or `/deepresearch` per question in an isolated workspace, then scores | Deterministic checks; no LLM judge | | Scoring | `done`, `cites`, `valid`, `title`, `recall`, `wall`, `tokens`, `cost` | See `evals/README.md` scores table | | Isolation | Fresh temp workspace and `FEYNMAN_HOME`; `FEYNMAN_TELEMETRY=0`; leftover process reaping | `run.mjs` `runQuestion` | | Provenance | Records git SHA, dirty flag, Feynman version, model, workdir, session JSONL | `run.mjs` `gitInfo`, result rows | | Results | Seven `.md`/`.jsonl` files, six configurations, 2026-09-23 to 2026-09-24 | `evals/results/` | The pipeline is: ```mermaid flowchart LR Q[question + key papers] --> I[isolated workspace
+ isolated FEYNMAN_HOME] I --> W["/lit or /deepresearch run"] W --> A[outputs/slug.md
+ provenance sidecar] A --> S[deterministic scorer] S --> M[citation validity
title overlap
key-paper recall] M --> R[result JSONL + Markdown table] ``` A crucial design choice: the eval measures the **artifact**, not the transcript. It reads the final Markdown, extracts arXiv IDs and DOIs, resolves them, and compares titles. It does not score the reasoning, the search path, the quality of the sources, or the truth of the prose. ### 2.1 The 12-question set | ID | Field | Question | Source | |---|---|---|---| | q01 | ML | test-time compute scaling for LLM reasoning | Feynman search benchmark | | q02 | ML | speculative decoding for LLM inference | Feynman search benchmark | | q03 | interpretability | sparse autoencoders for mechanistic interpretability | Feynman search benchmark | | q04 | genome editing | CRISPR base editing | Feynman search benchmark | | q05 | ML | mixture-of-experts routing | Feynman search benchmark | | q06 | NLP | retrieval-augmented generation | Feynman search benchmark | | q07 | genomics | enhancer–promoter compatibility, human vs. Drosophila | LitQA2 | | q08 | single-cell methods | tagmentation of cDNA directly in PCR mix | LitQA2 | | q09 | computational chemistry | Wyckoff-site constraints in symmetric MD | LitQA2 | | q10 | econometrics | difference-in-differences with staggered timing | hand-authored | | q11 | earth science | ML medium-range global weather forecasting | hand-authored | | q12 | cosmology | the Hubble tension | hand-authored | **Observation:** every committed result file uses only q01, q04, q07, and q10. The 0.5.3 Opus run uses q01 and q10. **Eight of the 12 questions (q02, q03, q05, q06, q08, q09, q11, q12) have no committed result.** The "12-question eval" is a design; the executed public benchmark is a four-question subset. --- ## 3. Strengths: what an eval engineer should copy These are not consolations. They are the parts of the harness that are genuinely better than the median agent eval. 1. **No LLM judge for the headline metric.** Citation validity and title match are deterministic. This avoids position, verbosity, and self-enhancement biases documented for LLM judges [6]. It also makes the scorer cheap to rerun. 2. **Per-question isolation.** Each run gets a fresh temp workspace and its own `FEYNMAN_HOME`, so one question cannot contaminate another through files or config. This is the right default and is exactly what my first verifier probe violated. 3. **Trace capture.** The result row records `git_sha`, `git_dirty`, `feynman_version`, model, `workdir`, per-question token usage, and the full session JSONL. That is enough to audit a run after the fact, even if the workdir is later deleted. 4. **Failures are retained.** Timed-out and incomplete rows are written to the JSONL and shown in the Markdown table rather than dropped. The baseline's 45-minute q10 timeout is visible, not hidden. 5. **Frozen-set discipline.** The README says: keep the set fixed; if you must change a question, bump the id rather than reuse one. That is the correct rule for longitudinal comparison. 6. **Self-aware caveats.** The README says a single run is noisy, tells the reader to inspect listed failures before calling something a hallucination, and lists the next metric lanes that are not built. This is unusually honest documentation. 7. **Low-cost verifier.** A verification pass on a six-paragraph draft cost 594,620 tokens and $0.0174 on `deepseek-v4.1-flash` in this environment. That is cheap enough to run on every draft, which is the right operating point for a verification layer. --- ## 4. Construct validity: what the numbers mean This is the central issue. The eval's metrics are sensible for what they measure, but the construct "research quality" is much larger than the measured construct "bibliographic integrity." | Metric | Code behavior | Measures | Does **not** measure | |---|---|---|---| | `done` | A final `outputs/.md` exists and a same-stem `.provenance.md` exists | Artifact production | Whether either file has content, or whether provenance fields are true | | `cites` | Distinct arXiv IDs and DOIs extracted by regex | Identifier-bearing citation density | Web citations, author–year citations, citation quality | | `valid` | Fraction of checked IDs that resolve via arXiv/Crossref/doi.org | Identifier existence | Whether the source supports the attached claim |
